uncited: This sets it apart from sibling methods like [Ray Marching with Reflections](1963-ray-marching-with-reflections.md) by specifically optimizing the traversal phase before shading, rather than optimizing the shading or reflection logic itself.
Cone Marching typically employs a two-pass architecture or a vertex-to-fragment data pipeline.

*   **Inputs:** Camera position ($ro$), camera direction/orientation, field of view (FOV), screen resolution, SDF scene function ($scene(p)$), maximum marching distance ($u\_maxDis$), and maximum steps ($u\_maxSteps$).
In the two-pass variant, the first pass outputs starting distances and step counts; the second pass outputs the final color.
**Setup Marching Plane:** Create a geometry representing the screen or marching plane.
*   Transform UV coordinates to clip space.
*   Unproject using the inverse projection matrix.
*   Transform to world space using the camera world matrix.
*   **Aspect Ratio Artifacts:** Using rectangular screen vertices without accounting for the camera aspect ratio causes uneven spacing and visual artifacts.
*   **Padding Factor:** The break condition uses a padding factor (1.25) on the cone radius.
Cone Marching was popularized in the context of real-time SDF rendering and fractal visualization.
